- When sentiment is consistently high (≥0.67) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 10–20% for high sentiment periods.
- If model shows sharp spikes (e.g., >50% increase from prior day), reduce forecast by 20–30% to avoid overshoot; especially if sentiment is mixed or declining.
- For low sentiment (≤0.33) or neutral sentiment, model often underestimates; increase forecast by 5–15% to compensate for mean reversion bias.
- Model tends to lag in early days of forecast horizon (e.g., 1–3 days ahead) — adjust upward by 5–10% for short-term (1–7 day) forecasts.
- If sentiment history shows strong upward momentum (e.g., 3+ consecutive high values), model often fails to capture the full rally — increase forecast by 10–20% for 10–30 day horizons.
- For 30-day forecasts, if true outcome exceeds model by >15% and sentiment is high, assume momentum is unsustainable — cap forecast at 1.2x model or adjust downward by 10–15%.
- If model forecast is consistently below true outcome (e.g., 3+ consecutive days), apply mean reversion correction: add 5–10% to forecast for next period if sentiment is neutral or slightly positive.
- If sentiment is volatile or mixed (alternating 0.33–0.67), model often overcorrects — reduce forecast by 5–10% to avoid overfitting to sentiment noise.
